extraction.chapter_summary: The narrator introduces Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a senseless, vicious, buffoonish landowner who rose from nothing to a fortune of a hundred thousand roubles. Married twice, he had three sons: Dmitri by his first wife Adelaïda Ivanovna, and Ivan and Alexey by his second. Adelaïda, a wealthy noblewoman of the Miüsov family, eloped with him, quickly came to despise him, and finally ran away with a divinity student to Petersburg, leaving the three-year-old Dmitri behind. When news came of her death, Fyodor reacted with both drunken joy and weeping.

extractions.title: Chapter II. He Gets Rid Of His Eldest Son

extraction.chapter_summary: After abandoning his infant son out of sheer forgetfulness, Fyodor Pavlovitch leaves three-year-old Mitya to be raised by the faithful family servant Grigory. Mitya's mother's cousin, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, returns from Paris and intervenes to take over the boy's education, becoming joint guardian, but soon forgets him too and passes him through a succession of relatives. Growing up believing he had property, Dmitri leads a wild, irregular life, and on coming of age discovers his father has whittled away his inheritance through doled-out installments and crafty agreements. A second visit confirms Dmitri has nothing left, leaving him beside himself and setting up the coming catastrophe.

events.summary: Fyodor Pavlovitch completely abandons his three-year-old son out of forgetfulness, and the servant Grigory takes Mitya into his care in the servant's cottage.
Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov returns from Paris, learns of Mitya's existence, and intervenes to undertake the child's education, becoming joint guardian with Fyodor Pavlovitch.
Miüsov leaves Mitya with a lady in Moscow and returns to Paris, forgetting the boy; Mitya is then passed through several households after the Moscow lady dies.
Dmitri grows up wild, fails out of the gymnasium, enters military school, fights a duel and is degraded to the ranks, and runs into debt expecting his inheritance.
On coming of age Dmitri meets his father for the first time to settle his property, takes a sum of money and signs agreements without obtaining any real account of the estate.
Four years later Dmitri returns to settle for good and discovers he has nothing left, has signed away his rights, and may even be in debt to his father, leaving him overwhelmed and suspecting deceit.

extractions.title: Chapter III. The Second Marriage And The Second Family

extraction.chapter_summary: Fyodor Pavlovitch marries his second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, a meek orphan girl, and torments her with debauchery until she dies after bearing him two sons, Ivan and Alexey. After her death the boys are abandoned like Mitya, then taken by the general's widow who raised Sofya; on her death she leaves them a legacy that the honest Yefim Petrovitch Polenov stewards and grows while educating them. The chapter traces Ivan's rise as a clever, proud student and writer, and the family's first-ever reunion in the town, with Ivan acting as a mysterious mediator between his father and Dmitri, while Alexey has already entered the monastery as a novice.

events.summary: Fyodor Pavlovitch marries Sofya Ivanovna, a meek orphan, by persuading her to elope; the general's widow gives no dowry and curses them both.
Fyodor Pavlovitch torments Sofya with orgies in her presence; Grigory takes her side, abuses his master, and drives the disorderly women out of the house.
Sofya bears two sons, Ivan and Alexey, falls into nervous illness, and dies when Alexey is in his fourth year, leaving the boys abandoned by their father and cared for by Grigory.
Three months after Sofya's death the general's widow arrives, slaps Fyodor Pavlovitch and shakes him by the hair, boxes Grigory's ear, and carries off both boys to raise them.
The old lady dies and wills the boys a thousand roubles each; Yefim Petrovitch Polenov honestly stewards the legacy, doubles it with interest, and educates both boys.
Ivan grows up clever and self-reliant, supporting himself at university through newspaper work and publishing a notorious article on ecclesiastical courts that reaches the monastery.

Ivan arrives in the town and lives amicably with his father for two months, acting as mediator between Fyodor Pavlovitch and Dmitri, whom he meets for the first time; the family is united for the first time.

extractions.title: Chapter IV. The Third Son, Alyosha

extraction.chapter_summary: This chapter introduces twenty-year-old Alyosha, the third son, characterizing him as an early lover of humanity who entered the monastery drawn by his attachment to the elder Zossima. It recounts his vivid childhood memory of his mother praying for him before an icon, his universally beloved yet dreamy and chaste nature, his upbringing under Yefim Petrovitch and later with distant relations, and his indifference to money (contrasted with Ivan). Returning home, he seeks his mother's grave (which Grigory, not Fyodor Pavlovitch, had marked), and the aged, increasingly debauched Fyodor Pavlovitch grows genuinely fond of him. The chapter closes with Fyodor Pavlovitch consenting to Alyosha becoming a novice, in a long drunken monologue about hell, hooks, and his own wickedness, moved that Alyosha is the only creature who has never condemned him.

extraction.chapter_summary: This chapter digresses from the narrative to characterize Alyosha as a robust, clear-eyed realist of nineteen rather than a sickly mystic, explaining why he chose the monastic path and his all-or-nothing faith in immortality. The narrator then explains the institution of "elders" in Russian monasteries—a voluntary, absolute submission of will undergone for self-conquest—and describes the elder Zossima, the celebrated, gentle elder to whom Alyosha is devoted and in whose cell Alyosha lives. The chapter recounts the people's adoration of Zossima and Alyosha's unquestioning faith in his holiness and miraculous power. Finally it sets up the impending family gathering in Zossima's cell, arranged on Fyodor Pavlovitch's joking suggestion amid the bitter discord between Dmitri and his father, which Alyosha awaits with dread for the elder's sake.

events.summary: The narrator defends Alyosha as a healthy, clear-eyed realist rather than a sickly mystic, and explains his all-or-nothing faith and choice of the monastic path.
The narrator digresses to explain the institution of 'elders' in Russian monasteries: voluntary, absolute submission of will, revived by Païssy Velitchkovsky and flourishing at Optin Monastery.
The narrator recounts legends illustrating an elder's unbounded authority, including the martyr's coffin cast from the church and a monk denied release even by the Patriarch at Constantinople.
Zossima, last of the monastery's elders and dying of illness, is described as gentle and beloved, drawing pilgrims who kiss his feet and seek healing.
Alyosha lives in Zossima's cell, holds unquestioning faith in his miraculous power and holiness, and dreams of the elder ushering in the Kingdom of Christ.
Fyodor Pavlovitch suggests, half in jest, that the discordant family gather in Zossima's cell to reconcile; Dmitri, Ivan, and Miüsov agree to attend and the day is fixed.
Zossima reluctantly consents to see the family, remarking 'Who has made me a judge over them?'; Alyosha dreads the visit and any affront to the elder, and sends Dmitri word to keep his promise.

themes.name: Faith versus realism
themes.description: Alyosha is presented as a realist whose faith springs not from miracles but from desire to believe, recasting belief as an act of will.

themes.name: Submission and spiritual authority
themes.description: The institution of elders demands total renunciation of one's will, a path to freedom that can also become Satanic pride.

themes.name: Holiness and the people's longing
themes.description: The Russian peasants' need to worship something holy and exalted is fulfilled in their adoration of the elder.

themes.name: Family discord
themes.description: The bitter strife between Dmitri and his father, and the disunity of the inharmonious Karamazov family, frames the impending gathering.

themes.name: All-or-nothing idealism
themes.description: Alyosha's refusal of compromise—living wholly for immortality or becoming an atheist—mirrors the seething youth's thirst for swift, total achievement.
